rating is what it may be.","fact_ids":["sec10-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Where is a tire's load rating printed, and what does it tell you?","fact_ids":["sec10-F07"]},"answer":{"text":"On the sidewall; A non-commercial Class C driver may tow a single vehicle or a combination as long as its gross vehicle weight rating does not exceed ten thousand pounds and the whole unit is seventy feet long or shorter. Drivers who want more towing information, or a J endorsement, should read the Nevada Non-Commercial A and B, J Endorsement Study Guide on the DMV website. We will then cover the weight terms and ratings every towing driver should know, and why loading a trailer wrongly or overloading it is dangerous for you and for others on the road.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Weight terms","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Gross vehicle weight: one vehicle and load.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R02"]},{"text":"Gross combination weight: the whole rig.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R02"]},{"text":"Rating: the maker's combined maximum.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Gross vehicle weight is the total weight of one vehicle plus its load, while gross combination weight is the total of the powered unit, its trailer or trailers, and the load. Gross combination weight rating is the manufacturer's stated combined loaded weight for a vehicle and the vehicle it tows. Axle weight is the weight one axle or one set of axles puts on the ground. So the weights describe what the vehicles actually weigh, and the rating describes the most the manufacturer says the combination should weigh when loaded. Keep the actual weight within the rating.","fact_ids":["sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Ratings on parts","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Tire load rating on the sidewall.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-R01"]},{"text":"Suspensions have weight ratings.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-R01"]},{"text":"Couplers have weight ratings.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"A tire's load rating, printed on its sidewall, is the most weight it can carry safely at a stated pressure; suspensions and coupling devices also carry maximum weight ratings. So the vehicle, the tires, the suspension and the hitch all have limits, and the safe load is the one that stays within every one of them. Gross combination weight is what the rig and load actually weigh, while the gross combination weight rating is the maximum combined loaded weight the manufacturer specifies. Checking the ratings before you load keeps you from overloading any one part of the rig.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Why loading matters","fact_ids":["sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Loose items can strike others.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},{"text":"Overloading hurts steering and braking.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},{"text":"Overworked brakes can fail.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Loading a trailer wrongly endangers you and others, since loose items can strike other road users and a quick stop or crash can damage the trailer's interior. Overloading hurts steering, braking and speed control: an overloaded rig crawls up hills, gains too much speed downhill, needs longer to stop, and its overworked brakes can fail. Keeping the load within the ratings and securing every item protects the rig, its contents, and every driver sharing the road with you. Secure every item and stay within the ratings for the vehicle, tires, suspension and coupler.","fact_ids":["sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Weight versus rating","fact_ids":["sec10-R01","sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Weight: what it actually weighs.","fact_ids":["sec10-R01","sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},{"text":"Rating: the maker's maximum.","fact_ids":["sec10-R01","sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},{"text":"Keep the weight under the rating.","fact_ids":["sec10-R01","sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. The terms gross combination weight and gross combination weight rating sound almost identical, so learners often treat them as one idea. They are different. Gross combination weight is what the rig and load actually weigh. The gross combination weight rating is the maximum combined loaded weight the manufacturer specifies for a vehicle and the vehicle it tows. One is a measurement, the other is a limit. When a question asks what the manufacturer sets, the answer is the rating; when it asks what the rig weighs right now, the answer is the weight.","fact_ids":["sec10-R01","sec10-F05","sec10-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check a tire rating","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"A tire's load rating.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-F01"]},{"text":"Where is it, and what does it mean?","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: where is a tire's load rating printed, and what does it tell you? Recall the rule before reading on. It is printed on the tire's sidewall, and it is the most weight the tire can carry safely at a stated pressure. Suspensions and coupling devices also carry maximum weight ratings, so the tires are only one of several limits on a towing rig. A Class C combination must also stay within the ten thousand pound weight rating and the seventy-foot length limit. Check each rating on the rig before you load it.","fact_ids":["sec10-F07","sec10-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Limits and weights recap","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R01","sec10-R02","sec10-F07","sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Class C: rating and length limits.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R01","sec10-R02","sec10-F07","sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},{"text":"Weight versus rating.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R01","sec10-R02","sec10-F07","sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]},{"text":"Overloading costs control.","fact_ids":["sec10-F01","sec10-F02","sec10-F05","sec10-F06","sec10-R01","sec10-R02","sec10-F07","sec10-F03","sec10-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To review, a non-commercial Class C driver may tow when the gross vehicle weight rating stays within ten thousand pounds and the whole unit is seventy feet or shorter, and the J endorsement study guide covers more. The height of the load, the weight on each axle and the balance from side to side all change how the rig steers, grips the road and resists rolling over. We will look at keeping the center of gravity low, the right amount of weight on the steering and driving axles, side-to-side balance and rollovers, the extra risks of flatbed trailers, and the pre-trip check of the load and compartment doors. Too little weight on the driving axles, for example, gives poor traction.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Keep it low","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"High center of gravity: rollover risk.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F11"]},{"text":"Cargo as low as possible.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F11"]},{"text":"Heaviest items underneath.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"The higher a load's center of gravity, the more likely the vehicle is to overturn, so keep cargo as low as possible and put the heaviest items underneath or in lower compartments. Uneven side-to-side loading can tip a trailer over, especially in turns; to prevent a rollover, take turns slowly and keep cargo close to the ground. Those two rules work together: a low, evenly spread load is the most stable, and slow turns give that load the best chance to stay upright. Stacking heavy items high, or all on one side, works against both rules at once.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Axle balance","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Too much on the steering axle: hard steering.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},{"text":"Too little: too light to steer.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},{"text":"Too little on drive axles: wheels spin.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard and can damage that axle and its tires, while too little weight up front can leave the steering axle too light to steer safely. Too little weight on the driving axles gives poor traction and lets the drive wheels spin easily. So balance runs front to back as well as side to side. The goal is enough weight on each axle to steer and grip, without overloading any one of them, which is why the load's position matters as much as its total weight. Spread the weight so every axle can do its job.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Flatbeds and pre-trip checks","fact_ids":["sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Flatbed loads can shift or fall.","fact_ids":["sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"Bad weather tests balance.","fact_ids":["sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"Doors latched, load secured.","fact_ids":["sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Flatbed trailers carry a greater risk of the load shifting sideways or falling off, and in bad weather a poorly balanced rig may not stay balanced. Pre-trip, make sure the load is balanced and secured and every outside storage compartment door is latched or locked. The pre-trip check covers both halves of the job: the load must be balanced and secured so it cannot shift, and every outside storage compartment door must be latched or locked. Flatbeds call for the most care, because a load on an open deck is the one most likely to slide sideways or fall off.","fact_ids":["sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Front-axle weight","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Too much: hard steering, damage.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},{"text":"Too little: unsafe steering.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},{"text":"Aim for balance.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Some drivers think putting extra weight up front always improves steering. It does not. Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard and can damage that axle and its tires. Too little weight up front, usually from shifting the load too far back, can leave the steering axle too light to steer safely. Both extremes are unsafe. And at the other end of the rig, too little weight on the driving axles gives poor traction and lets the drive wheels spin. Balanced weight is the answer every time. Balance is the goal.","fact_ids":["sec10-F09","sec10-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the drive axles","fact_ids":["sec10-F10","sec10-F09","sec10-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Too little drive-axle weight.","fact_ids":["sec10-F10","sec10-F09","sec10-F08"]},{"text":"What happens?","fact_ids":["sec10-F10","sec10-F09","sec10-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: what happens when the driving axles carry too little weight? Recall the rule before reading on. Traction is poor, and the drive wheels spin easily. That is one of three balance problems in this lesson: too much steering-axle weight makes steering hard, too little leaves it too light to steer safely, and too little on the driving axles costs traction. A high center of gravity adds a fourth, the risk of overturning, which is why heavy items go low and underneath. Keep cargo low and the weight balanced.","fact_ids":["sec10-F10","sec10-F09","sec10-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Loading recap","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F09","sec10-F10","sec10-F11","sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Heavy items low.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F09","sec10-F10","sec10-F11","sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"Balance front to back and side to side.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F09","sec10-F10","sec10-F11","sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]},{"text":"Secure the load before every trip.","fact_ids":["sec10-F08","sec10-F09","sec10-F10","sec10-F11","sec10-R05","sec10-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, keep the center of gravity low by putting the heaviest items underneath or in lower compartments. Balance the weight so the steering axle is neither overloaded nor too light, and so the driving axles have enough weight for traction. Load evenly side to side, take turns slowly and keep cargo close to the ground to prevent rollovers. Flatbed loads can shift or fall off, and a poorly balanced rig may not stay balanced in bad weather. if it is not, the coupling is not properly seated.","fact_ids":["sec10-F16","sec10-F17"]},"result":{"text":"The driver checks the locking lever, then confirms there is no gap and the trailer sits flat on the skid plate.","fact_ids":["sec10-F16","sec10-F17"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking one inspection before leaving covers a whole long trip.","fact_ids":["sec10-F19"]},"correction":{"text":"Re-inspect within the first fifty miles, again after three hours or one hundred fifty miles, and ideally at every break.","fact_ids":["sec10-F19"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Fifty miles, then three hours or one-fifty.","fact_ids":["sec10-F19"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"On a ball coupler, what must the safety chains be before you drive away?","fact_ids":["sec10-F13"]},"answer":{"text":"Attached and crossed.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13"]},"rationale":{"text":"When hitching a ball coupler, the ball must be seated firmly, the safety latch secured down, and the safety chains attached and crossed.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec10-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Hitching safely","fact_ids":["sec10-R03","sec10-F13","sec10-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ball hitches.","fact_ids":["sec10-R03","sec10-F13","sec10-F15"]},{"text":"Fifth-wheel hitches.","fact_ids":["sec10-R03","sec10-F13","sec10-F15"]},{"text":"Testing and re-inspecting.","fact_ids":["sec10-R03","sec10-F13","sec10-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers hitching a trailer and inspecting it. We will look at load-distributing hitches, the checks for a ball-and-hitch coupler, the fifth-wheel hitch and its checks, how to test the connection before you leave, and when to inspect the trailer again during a long trip. A ball-and-hitch coupler joins a ball on the tow vehicle to a coupler on the trailer tongue, whereas a fifth-wheel hitch sits in a truck bed and locks onto a kingpin and is less prone to balance problems. Each type has its own list of things to confirm before you drive.","fact_ids":["sec10-R03","sec10-F13","sec10-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Ball couplers","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14","sec10-R04","sec10-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ball seated, latch down.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14","sec10-R04","sec10-F12"]},{"text":"Chains attached and crossed.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14","sec10-R04","sec10-F12"]},{"text":"Pin and clip locked; lines clear.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14","sec10-R04","sec10-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"When hitching a ball coupler, the ball must be seated firmly in the coupler, the coupler safety latch secured down, and the safety chains attached and crossed. The ball mount must be locked into the tow vehicle's receiver with its pin and clip or other locking device, and the electric lines must be seated, locked and free of tangles or dragging. Before towing with a ball hitch, confirm every coupling part is present and unbroken and the trailer tongue is not bent, cracked or damaged. A load-distributing hitch spreads the tongue load across all axles to steady the tow vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec10-F13","sec10-F14","sec10-R04","sec10-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Fifth-wheel hitches","fact_ids":["sec10-F15","sec10-F16","sec10-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mounts in the truck bed.","fact_ids":["sec10-F15","sec10-F16","sec10-R06"]},{"text":"Very stable, but fills the bed.","fact_ids":["sec10-F15","sec10-F16","sec10-R06"]},{"text":"Lock brakes; lock the lever.","fact_ids":["sec10-F15","sec10-F16","sec10-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"A fifth-wheel hitch mounts in a pickup bed and couples to the trailer's kingpin; it is very stable but uses most of the bed and needs the space behind it kept clear for turns. Before backing under a fifth-wheel trailer, lock the trailer brakes, and after the jaws close around the kingpin, make sure the locking lever is locked, or the coupling is not properly seated. Check that the mounting assembly is solidly attached with no loose or missing parts and that the kingpin is not bent. Those checks confirm the hitch itself is sound before you rely on it.","fact_ids":["sec10-F15","sec10-F16","sec10-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec10-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Fifth-wheel coupling checks","fact_ids":["sec10-F17","sec10-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"No gap between couplings.","fact_ids":["sec10-F17","sec10-R07"]},{"text":"Trailer flat on the skid plate.","fact_ids":["sec10-F17","sec10-R07"]},{"text":"Lines intact; release arm engaged.","fact_ids":["sec10-F17","sec10-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"A coupled fifth wheel must have no gap between the upper and lower coupling, the trailer must sit flat on the skid plate, and the plate must be greased as required. Fifth-wheel electric lines must not be chafed, spliced or worn, the platform supporting the skid plate must be free of cracks, and the release arm must be engaged with any safety latch in place. A gap, a tilted trailer or a disengaged release arm all point to a coupling that is not seated, so fix any of them before you move the coupled unit.
